The Unsolved CatalogueHelp
Solve!pick one below

Historical cipher letters that nobody has read. Pick one, open its page, and give that page’s address to your AI agent: the page holds the sources, what has been tried and the instructions.

  1. 1pick a row
  2. 2open its page
  3. 3point your agent at the URL
  4. 4send back what it finds
On this pageWhere things stand, 29 Oct 2026Numbers that have left the catalogueAbout the catalogueHow the scores were set
Many of these cannot be read from a desk. 177 of the open entries are marked needs archive scans: the ciphertext, or the key material that would unlock it, is not online, so nothing can be deciphered until the archive digitises it or someone photographs it in the reading room. They are listed because a request to the archive, or a visit, is the first step.

5.018 Jun 1592no. 15● Charles III of Lorraine to the count of Vaudémont, copyattempted, openLorraine's double game between the League and Henri IV. The ciphered passages carry the military business the clear text only skirts: prisoners and munitions, an order to receive the Duke's commandment and to conserve the plain, Chasteauvillain, and the intention to bring the army back into the quarters of La Fauche, between Neufchateau and Chaumont. The clear text around them has the attempt on Chasteauvillain, munitions promised and undelivered, Chaumont and Buzonville; no. 22's decipherment carries the January business - the Spanish march on Rouen, Mayenne finding the Spaniards resolved on battle, Parma's judgement, then the legate, the Spanish pretensions, Villeroy at Pontoise, the house of Bourbon, Bellievre, and the peace.BnF fr. 3621 no. 97 (fol. 109); no. 22 (fol. 31) is the January deciphermentbtv1b52524472nB

Where things stand, 29 Oct 2026

Before starting on an entry, read its known and open lines on its page and the open pull requests below. Work that has landed is folded into both lists at each rebuild; work still in a pull request is not. If a number you were given is not in the table, it has left the catalogue: look it up. The lists and the pull requests are recomputed at every rebuild; each entry’s known and open lines were written by hand and carry the day they were checked (all of them on 21 Oct 2026 at the latest full pass).

What is solved or known so far

173 catalogue numbers have been deciphered, explained or found in print and have left the open list (the list; every write-up is on the write-ups page). 83 of the entries still open have pieces already deciphered or identified.

the 83 open entries with known pieces
  • no. 5 Nicolas Raince (Rome) to Montmorency and François I, eight letters May–Dec 1526; Aug 1529 — Tomokiyo's 1526 key fits after re-measuring (raince.html); the clear close of 13 May transcribed.
  • no. 7 Hieronimo Ranzo (?) to 'Garbino', intercepted imperial letter 11 Apr 1528 — No. 6 (del Vasto, Cipher 2) deciphered here with Lasry's key, 98.0% (vasto1527.html); no. 10 (Cipher 1) key recovered by Lasry 2023, read in part with Tomokiyo's text. No. 20: Ranzo's code key recovered from ciphertext only by George Lasry and, independently, Paolo Rosson (6 Oct 2026); no. 20 measured here at 94.4% (ranzo1528.html, PRs #35, #45).
  • no. 9 Espagnol 318 nos. 92, 93, 94: Ferdinand's secretariat ciphers (Great Captain 1500, Suárez de Figueroa 1504, viceroy of Sicily 1503) 24 Feb 1504 — Nothing for nos. 93 and 94: keys not identified; a homophonic anneal of 1,016 signs of no. 93 failed (esp318no93.html). Former siblings: no. 5 printed by Parisi 2020 (federico1497), no. 92 about 75% deciphered with the Cifra general (esp318), no. 95 recto deciphered in full by George Lasry with his own key (esp318no95, PR #75).
  • no. 10 Noailles (Venice) to the Cardinal de Lorraine 13 Nov 1558 — The court's decipherment of the time stands in the inner margin of f. 60r (partly legible) and in the outer margin of f. 60v (nearly complete) (noailles1558.html). Transcribed and key largely recovered by Michael Brackx (issue #113, Oct 2026), read in part as he grades it; not yet reproduced here. Former siblings: Seure's 1558 Lisbon letters, key recovered by Angus Robinson (PR #40, seure1558); La Guiche 1551, key recovered ciphertext-only here (guiche1551).
  • no. 11 Catherine de Médicis and the Court to the bishop of Rennes 31 Jul 1563; 1560s — Tomokiyo's key fits after calibration on the glossed sibling f. 57 (rennes1563.html); La Ferrière 1885 prints f. 55 with the cipher left blank.
  • no. 13 Anonymous to the Duke of Mercœur 'ce xxvj juin' [c. 1586] — Clear frame transcribed; cipher shown not to be in Lasry's 2022 fr. 15564 key (as Lasry himself found), nor the Mayenne-Forget or Clair. 357 keys (mercoeur1586.html).
  • no. 15 Charles III of Lorraine to the count of Vaudémont, copy 18 Jun 1592 — Letter-pair key recovered from the ciphertext alone (lorraine1592.html).
  • no. 17 Henri IV to Maisse (Venice), two letters (fr. 16093 ff. 406, 410) 1593 — Clear copies located in Brienne 13 (NAF 6984 ff. 171r, 193v; maisse1593.html). ff. 370 and 373 deciphered from the existing decipherment (maisse1592).
  • no. 19 Diego de Ibarra, Spanish despatch of 1593 (fr. 3984 no. 68) Feb–Jul 1593 — Tomokiyo's Feria-Mansfeld key decodes the syllabic figures (ibarra1593.html).
  • no. 20 Cardinal Sega's legation: the Curia's instruction and a Paris letter 14–15 May 1593 — Nos. 6 and 8: Brice Dudout described both systems and gives partial candidate readings (bdudout.github.io); Tomokiyo (Cryptologia 43(1) 2019) gave a preliminary decipherment of 1593 figure texts, probably incl. no. 6. Former siblings: Baudouin-Desportes ff. 186, 189 deciphered by Paolo Rosson with Tomokiyo's key (desportes1593.html); Mauclerc letters deciphered at the time (mauclerc1593).
  • no. 21 Nevers to Revol and to Pisany, seven copies 27 Aug – 23 Oct 1593 — Key no. 46 fits the Pisany letters (nevers1593.html); key no. 60 identified for the Revol letters (revol1593.html); the 31 Aug Instruction is a double crib (Memoires de Nevers ii, 492-499).
  • no. 30 Champagne news-letters to Nevers, June 1590 (fr. 3623 nos. 24, 25, 60) and no. 78 Jun 1590; 1591 — Two-digit alphabet of nos. 24/25/60 rebuilt from glossed figures (63 of 104 figures valued; champagne1590.html); no decipherment or clear copy found.
  • no. 36 King Frederick II (the Great) of Prussia (1712-1786) (London) to Louis Michell (1712-1786), Prussian resident in London 28 Dec 1751 — Envoy-code table from R1050/R1051 matches R1955 (95 of 360 groups valued; r1955.html).
  • no. 46 János Pápai (Belgrade) to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 6 March 1710: graphic-sign passages 6 Mar 1710 — R731's six passages transcribed tentatively (~330 signs); a control-validated solver finds no Hungarian (papai1710.html). Former siblings: Pápai's eleven numeric letters deciphered with envoy key R580, 99.7% (papai1706.html).
  • no. 53 Heinrich Anton von Zeschau (Dresden) to Albin Leo von Seebach, 4 ciphertexts 18 Jan 1841 – 26 Oct 1843 — System identified as a two-digit syllabary; R5005 transcribed (3,969 digits); seven values (11 la, 70 pre, 82 m, 34 i, 29 er, 40 e, 46 que) recovered from the rubbed-out pencil decipherment (zeschau1841.html).
  • no. 57 TNA SP 106/10: the codebreaker's "Venetian Cifer", c. 1623-24 (R664, R660) undated — The codebreaker's grid R658 gives 102 values of the code (sp106box10.html).
  • no. 58 English royalist letter in numerical code, September 1645 (SP 106/10 f. 251) Sept 1645 — R931 identified as a 1645 royalist nomenclator letter (~190 numbers, 104 distinct, clear words); Lasry's 1645-46 SP 106 keys, the R932 Goring key and the Charles I-Culpeper key R9117/R9118 excluded (sp106r931.html).
  • no. 66 A Venetian secretary to the Venetian ambassador in England, 1625, in a three-figure syllabic code (SP 106/10 ff. 193-195) first half of 1625 — R722 identified (Venetian secretary to the ambassador, first half of 1625); endorsement and clear Italian passages read; all 420 code groups transcribed; four values from clear-text junctions and some from the codebreaker's partial key R701 p. 3 (sp106r722.html).
  • no. 74 Palm (London) to Starhemberg, German letter with ciphered passages, 1727 14 Mar 1727 — A few groups glossed at the time (33=e, 23=n, 10=d, 15=t, 40=long s, 230=der); R7928 shown not to be Palm's key (palm1727.html). PR #21 (Feyseel): a word solver that recovers synthetic texts finds no German in R7927, pointing to the transcription.
  • no. 78 Paris 1719 code letters, 2 ciphertexts 7 and 10 Feb 1719 — R2963 and R2974 deciphered at the time (dropped). In R2964 about 33 of 354 groups carry contemporary glosses (bl32305.html). Carré letters split to entry 70.
  • no. 87 Henry Percy to Secretary Cecil 23 Jul 1559 — Deciphered at the time by Cecil on the original, TNA SP 52/1 (calendared CSP Foreign I 1051; Bain, CSP Scotland I 501). Not deciphered here from the Forbes tracing (percy1559.html).
  • no. 92 Catherine de' Medici to Paul de Foix, French ambassador in London, intercepted letter 15 Jan 1563 — R9238 (Coligny, 12 Jan 1563) deciphered at the time, in CSP Foreign vi and Forbes (coligny1563). R9241: key identified as Paul de Foix's own cipher, Tomokiyo's 1565 reconstruction (Feyseel Nur, PR #21); partial decipherment by Lawrence Beck (PRs #18, #27), converging with it (targets/foix1563, no page).
  • no. 97 Throckmorton leaf 1559: marginal word-sign code, and John Wood to Cecil 1568 10 Jul 1559 – 8 Aug 1559 — Throckmorton's 10 July 1559 letter on f. 32 decoded about 85% here (decoded, not read since 23 Oct 2026) with Tomokiyo's Cipher 1 key plus corrections (throck1559.html). The margin code (throck1559margin.html) and Wood's line (wod1568.html) are written up as not deciphered.
  • no. 120 Nicholas Wotton to Queen Mary, 13 June 1554 Jun 1554 — Key DECODE R354 matched (harley1582r8499.html).
  • no. 121 "L'Estat du Roy de Navarre et de son party en France" (unknown author) after 1580 — Homophonic sign alphabet recovered from the ciphertext alone; all clear text transcribed (harley1582r8505.html).
  • no. 123 Walsingham to Burghley (letter-book copy) 20 Jan 1572/3 — Clear letter-book copy, printed in Digges 1655 p. 313 with the cipher unread; Dieppe fits the port by context only as a guess (walsingham1572.html).
  • no. 125 Walsingham letter-book, Nov 1572 (Burghley, Leicester, Walsingham): name codes Nov 1572 — Four clear letters, printed in Digges 1655 pp. 297-301; code [3] = the Queen by context (r8361.html).
  • no. 127 Burghley to Walsingham (letter-book copy) 5 Jul 1572 — Clear letter-book copy, printed in Digges 1655 (July 1572); code [3] = the French King by context (r8358.html).
  • no. 128 Lord Burghley (Audley End) to Francis Walsingham, ambassador in France 2 Sep 1571 — Clear letter-book copy, printed in Digges 1655 pp. 123-124; nothing deciphered (targets/burghley1572, no page; DECODE date 1572 corrected to 1571).
  • no. 129 Walsingham to Burghley, 25 June 1571 (letter-book; with Elizabeth to Walsingham, clear) Jun 1571 — Elizabeth's letter is clear; Walsingham's letter is printed in Digges 1655 p. 106 with the cipher as figures (r8356.html).
  • no. 131 Cobham (Belgia) to Walsingham, 4 ciphertexts 1588 – 9 Jun 1588 — Partial alphabet from the glossed siblings R8488, R8493 (cobham1588.html).
  • no. 135 Charles I to Prince Charles, 1 Aug 1648 (cipher passage) 1 Aug 1648 — Printed without the cipher in Halliwell 1846. The Biermann-Bosbach-Brown 1648 key (which deciphered four other Isle of Wight letters in 2021) and the Titus key are excluded (targets/charlesi, no page).
  • no. 137 Abraham Cowley's hand ('Mr. Conleys Hand'), Paris, to a royalist in Holland, 2 letters 28 Dec 1652 – 3 May 1653 — Clear text of both letters read; docket identifies Abraham Cowley's hand, not 'Conley' (conley1652.html). Hyde-Barwick key ruled out.
  • no. 152 Pandolfo Malatesta, archbishop of Patras, to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga 22 April 1428 — Clear Latin frame read. The other three letters of R1854 deciphered here: image 2 (r1854, key from ciphertext), image 3 (mutiliana1428), images 4-5 (cattanei1430) (malatesta1428.html).
  • no. 157 Giuliano Caprile (Eger) to Bonaventura Pistofilo, 9 March 1519 9 Mar 1519 — R1129-R1135 deciphered in 1882 (Vestigia b/c copies) or interlined. The 1520-21 letters: key recovered from Somogyi 2025's plaintext, V1921 97%, R1139 89.7%, R1136 66.9% (caprile1520.html). R1128 written up as not deciphered (caprile1519.html). The 1519 key was reconstructed by ASMo archivists in the 19th century; sheets printed small in Cremonini 2017, figs. 17.1-17.3 (ASMo Cifrario b. 8 fasc. 4); pointer from Michael Brackx, issue #121.
  • no. 161 Bavarian key volume: letter to Duke Wilhelm V (1583), unread 1583 — 12 of 14 records deciphered here and split: kaa4591 (System A', 89.8%), kaa4591b (Łaski's cipher; R9322, R9417, R9403 over the bar), fulda1576 (known key), r9367 (known key; decoded, not read since 23 Oct 2026), r9416 (key from ciphertext, 6%). r9424 (key recovered ciphertext-only by Ryan Xu, 23 Oct 2026; read in part).
  • no. 166 Principe di Castelcicala to Naples, an undated letter in a second code (R9588) undated (1816–23?) — R9588: 432 groups transcribed, sparse pencil syllabic glosses noted (r9586.html). Former siblings in the Segreteria di Stato code: key rebuilt from four interlinear decipherments, 46.7% of groups valued, no letter reads through (castelcicala1816.html).

Below the 95 % bar; the unread part is the nomenclator.

What is still unsolved

1111 entries are open (1097 counted targets, the rest also noted): 37 in progress here (a target folder is working on them; its notes are linked from the entry’s page), 27 blocked from outside (no images online, an archive order needed, or no key known to exist), 80 attempted here without a decipherment, 967 not yet attempted. 3 have their key material at hand and no outside blocker (no. 157, no. 166, no. 167): good places to start.

the 1111 open entries, by priority, with what is still open
  • no. 1314 Marcolino Barbavara → Francesco Sforza, the ducal secretary's cipher letters from Rimini and Rome 13 Feb - 4 May 1447 — Mazzatinti 'In cifre'; key on DECODE (R1857).
  • no. 1307 Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan → Francesco Sforza, six cipher letters on parchment, Nov-Dec 1446 1 Nov - 31 Dec 1446 — DECODE Non-decrypted (all six; DECODE gives no sender or receiver, identified here from Mazzatinti). Not in the repo: targets/it1583 viewed R7900-R7915 on 23 Oct 2026 and found none in the f. 68/70 alphabet, but did not work them. f. 131 (not a DECODE record) is a contemporary translation of f. 130, and BnF ital. 1584 (1447) has more Duke's cipher letters each followed by a 'Traduzione' (ff. 5/6, 8/9): cribs for the Duke's cipher of these months.
  • no. 1312 Filippo Maria Visconti → Francesco Sforza, ducal cipher slips on parchment (the last months of the Visconti duke) Nov 1446 - 23 Mar 1447 — Mazzatinti: 'In cifre: membran.' for each; 'Traduzione della lettera precedente' only after ff. 5, 8 (1584) and 130 (1583). Image check: f. 15 is followed by a clear f. 16 of the same date (probably its decipherment, unlisted). ital. 1583 ff. 110, 136 are DECODE R7902, R7907 (Non-decrypted). The ital. 1583 slips (ff. 110, 136, 162; DECODE R7902, R7907) are catalogued separately with the other ital. 1583 Visconti letters (venice_milan_decode row 0); this entry is the ital. 1584 slips.

Brev från C.W. von Düben till N.P. Gyldenstolpe och Lovisa Ulrika 1764-1765 ... Chiffernycklar." Not on DECODE (no Lovisa Ulrika record), not in the repo. No decipherment seen on the sampled pages; interlinear decipherment not checked page by page. The 24 Oct Riksarkivet sweep listed K 259 as keys only; the 26 Oct sample (image 107) shows a full page of numeric cipher. 27 Oct 2026, Brice Dudout (email): Frederick II's letter of 3 March 1765 in this group is printed in the Politische Correspondenz, vol. 24, no. 15458 (one letter; Düben's code letters unaffected; targets/duben1764/).
  • no. 465 Conrad Biermann's copybook of outgoing letters to Danish ministers abroad, "a large part in cipher" 1675-1676 — Daisy (new search): "En stor del af de indførte skrivelser er i chifre." Viewed one opening (image 109): ciphertext copied into the register, clear text around it, no decipherment. Not on DECODE, not in the repo. Key lead: Tyske Kancelli "Chiffer" 1670-1709 (heid 2132747, "a mix of many different cipher keys"), fully scanned (epid 15553654). 27 Oct 2026, Brice Dudout (email): Copenhagen to Just Høeg at The Hague, 2, 5 and 9 January 1675, read: 841 of 849 groups, key = the untitled sheet at image 55 of the TKUA 'Chiffer' volume 1670-1709, checked on letters to Meyercrone in Paris in the same key. The rest of the copybook not reported. Extended 27 Oct 2026 (Europe chiffrée, documents.html#hoeg-1675, #meyercrone-1675): 37 letters read with key K55, 18 to Høeg (2 Jan-5 June 1675) and 19 to Meyercrone (16 Feb-21 June; 6,103 groups, 99.4%). Still open: the letters to Lilienkron (German, numbers 14-707 with the signs Δ θ), to Gioë and Schröder (K55 family, untested) and the letter of 2 Jan to Meyercrone (another key); see the survey in targets/biermann1675/.   • no. 597 Anhalt-Dessau agents in Prague → Prince Johann Georg I: Johann von Alairt's letters of 1610-11 in upside-down German, deciphered at the time except a slip of Nov 1611; the prince's cipher table and a slip key are unused 1604-1611 — The Nov 1611 slip; whether any letter uses the prince's table or the slip key.
  • no. 637 John J. Appleton → John Quincy Adams, Cadiz, despatch with an 18-group coded passage on the Spanish liberal government's secret English loan, printed 'no decodification' 6 Aug 1823 — Manning, Diplomatic Correspondence ... Independence of the Latin-American Nations (1925) vol. 3, doc. 1124, p. 2041, prints the groups with '[no decodification]'. The groups fit the code rebuilt in targets/jqa (the = 1385, of = 1576, that = 1384, and = 668; the London/St Petersburg code): with targets/jqa/code_table.tsv 16 of 18 groups take a value ('... of [794] that ... was [192] and that he had a part in England'). Not in the repo (known.py: Appleton no hits).
  • no. 681 Lt. Gen. Richard Taylor (Dept. of Alabama, Mississippi and East Louisiana) → Maury, S. D. Lee, Forrest and others: telegram letter-books with Confederate Vigenère passages copied in cipher only Nov 1864 - Apr 1865 — Not unsolved in the strict sense: the keys are the known Confederate ones. Frame 0061 transcribed from the image and read here with COME RETRIBUTION (Vigenère, key running through the cipher letters only): 'Telegraph in cipher what [cavalry you have on which side of bay, strength and name of commander] ... Direct [cavalry so keep close to enemy] as possible ... [keep in constant telegraphic communication with] Genl D W Adams ... indicate in cipher [what] ... you have decided upon [outside through which to communicate]'. On the OCR alone, runs in vol. 11 read with COME RETRIBUTION ('stores', 'will move westward', 'was evacuated by') and runs in vol. 10 read with COMPLETE VICTORY ('Genl Johnston this alone will restore confidence', 'renders the assignment'). The volumes carry the 'War Records COPIED' stamp, so the Official Records may print these telegrams, but whether OR printed the cipher words deciphered or left them out was not checked. Not on DECODE; known.py: no hit for Come Retribution, Taylor 1865 or Markoe. 27 Oct 2026 (WAINUT, PR #111; targets/taylor1865/, in progress): four telegrams of 12 and 30 Mar and 6 and 8 Apr 1865 read from the NARA images with COME RETRIBUTION; the 6 and 8 April ones are printed in clear in the OR. Frame 0061's "on each side of bay" and "[?west] point" confirmed.
  • no. 885 Sigismund August of Poland, Frater Georg Martinuzzi and Queen Isabella to Ibrahim Pasha: ciphered copies with a Latin exemplar 1 Jun - 22 Jul 1548 — AIS: the cipher copies are not described as deciphered, but each letter has a Latin exemplar of the same text. Malvezzi's covering letters are edited in Austro-Turcica 1541-1552 (7-4-9: pp. 276-278); the edition may not print the enclosures. Not on DECODE; not in the repo (known.py: '7-4-5' no hits).
  • no. 989 Sir Henry Bennet to Sir Richard Fanshawe: eight pages of cipher, not deciphered, 'but the key for which is amongst the papers' 6 Oct 1664 — HMC: 'Eight pages of cipher, not deciphered, but the key for which is amongst the papers. They prove to be the cipher part of the letter dated August 25th in the printed letters (p. 283)'. So the plaintext is in print: a ready crib.
  • no. 1335 Carlo Bascapè → Carlo Borromeo, letters from Spain with numeric code passages; cipher key filed in the same series 22 Aug, 29 Aug and 3 Dec 1580 — OPAC: "Ep. in cifra" / "Lettera in cifra" (F 58 inf. 247, 249); F 57 inf. 149 "contiene parte cifrata (c. 193r); la cifra per la decodifica si trova alle cc. 314v-315r (n. 275)". Viewed f. 367r (code groups in a clear letter) and f. 314r of the key (faint). No decipherment noted on the letters. F 61 inf. n. 267 (Rovato) also refers to the same cifrario. Not on DECODE; no repo hit.
  • no. 761 James Wilkinson ('Agent 13') ↔ Spanish governors of Louisiana: cipher letters in two dictionary-and-table codes, most pages unread c. 1789-1806 (letters undated in the released transcriptions) — Partly read. Chu, Valenti and Knight (EMNLP Findings 2020, arXiv 2010.04746) recovered 75.1% of cipher-word tokens on a held-out 500-token excerpt (LoC 3044-3045) by a known-plaintext wordbank from the deciphered pages plus a neural LM; the dictionary itself was never identified and the 1096 system was not attacked. Not in the repo (known.py: no hits for 2374, Papeles de Cuba, Wilkinson cipher). Not on DECODE as far as checked.

The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online. The text is Spanish, not German. The carriers were the cousins Henry Kolbeck and Olga de (d') Visser, detained at Laredo on 14 Feb 1917 (the 22 Feb date is not checked). Kolbeck confessed in April 1917 that he wrote the document himself (complaint under s. 37 of the Penal Code, May 1917). Read by the Bureau in 1917; that reading is not located.

Pickering to Hamilton 18 Jun 1799: Rozier showed his cipher and Pickering checked some coded passages against Rozier's plain copies. So the Rozier letters were checked in part with the writer's own key; the other letters in the packet and a full decipherment are not recorded. The letter counts of the groups are those of German plaintext with X as word separator (pooled IC 0.060 on noisy OCR, top letters E R X I N A), so this is a transposition, not Enigma. Tested 27 Oct 2026: the 1939 exercise message reads in full with its key card (double columnar transposition, key a then b, the group containing the Kenngruppe 'fks' at group 7 dropped, CH written Q): 'ROEM X ERSTE FLAKREGIMENT X ZWOELF X RES X FLAKABTEILUNG ... WERDEN IN DER NACHT DURQ TEILE DER X FLAKTRANSPORTABTEILUNG X DREIEINS X NAQ X MAGDEBURG X VERLEGT X LUFTGAUKOMMANDO X ROEM X DREI' (dw1939.py). The 1940 messages carry no key and no decipherment on the frames; some have a typed Fernschreiben in clear on a neighbouring frame (e.g. 862, 4 June 1940) that may be the same text.

Friedman wrote in 1948 that the Riverbank cipher records were thought destroyed after Fabyan's death (Cora Tyzzer letter, NSA A69876) and that the LoC Fabyan collection held none of them; the NYPL boxes came via Fabyan's widow to George Curtis (gift 1960), so these two boxes may be the only survivors. MI-8 broke several Mexican government codes in 1917-19 (repo: research/nara_triage_c/e), so many messages will be read; whether any are unread is unknown. Schmeh (2018) saw three boxes, not these. NSA historians (Dave Hatch and a colleague, a November visit, year not given) went through all nine Riverbank boxes and found them 'very duplicative and mixed': page proofs of Riverbank publications, student folders and exercises on graph paper, a few Parker Hitt letters; no cipher intercepts are mentioned (NSA blog 'A great TDY', Doc ID 6919113, released 30 Mar 2026).

  • no. 137 Abraham Cowley's hand ('Mr. Conleys Hand'), Paris, to a royalist in Holland, 2 letters 28 Dec 1652 – 3 May 1653 — The 23 code numbers in five runs (names, a place). Blocker: too few for ciphertext-only; needs a Jermyn/Queen key of 1652-53.
  • no. 721 Letter in cypher from Leavenworth, Kansas, in the Jack Downing (Cherokee) file, 1916 4 Jun 1916 — Index card only; nothing says it was read. Leavenworth suggests a federal prisoner's letter. known.py: no hit.
  • no. 775 Henry Gibbs → Margaret Fitch, courtship letter no. 16 with passages in code 1738 (letter no. 16 of the series 27 Dec 1737 - 19 Dec 1738) — Finding aid: "At several crucial junctures in letter 16, Henry resorted to the use of a code to disguise passages dealing with an apparently embarrassing encounter with a newly married friend." No decipherment noted.
  • no. 776 T. C. Connor journal, references to acquaintances in a pictographic code 1825-1826 — Finding aid: "Some references to Connor's acquaintances are made in a pictographic code." No reading noted.
  • no. 777 John H. Tyler → Daniel H. London (Richmond fabric merchant), business letters using a code May-July 1852 — Finding aid: "another correspondent, John H. Tyler, utilized a code in his letters from May-July 1852." Type of code (a few code words or a cipher) not stated.
  • no. 778 Coleman Blach → Rosa Blach, love letters with a code for his clients spring-summer 1894 — Finding aid: "using a code when discussing specific clients." No reading noted.
  • no. 1420 Code telegrams not understood (2nd Military District, Sydney) 1916 — Title only; probably garbled military code telegrams.
  • no. 70 Letters to Mr Carré, Pall Mall, 1742–45, 3 ciphertexts Mar 1742 – 19 Jan 1745 — All three letters. Blocker: no key, gloss or crib; a random-order code of this size cannot be rebuilt ciphertext-only.
  • no. 193 Bayard to Montmorency 5 Jan 1526 — The three cipher lines (56 signs of 29 kinds). Blocker: no key, too short; needs the original (V. 41 f. 4).
  • no. 206 Murberg, Johan, Görtz, Georg Heinrich von to unknown recipient 1717 — All five cipher passages (809 groups). Blocker: no key; ciphertext-only failed even on a synthetic control; needs Görtz's German chancery key (Riksarkivet).
  • no. 353 Duke of Ormond to the Earl of Arran, short passage in code ('a trial whether you are skilful in deciphering') 24 Jan 1677/8 — All 20 numbers: not deciphered; the 1678 Ormond-Arran code is not rebuilt and the manuscript (Ormonde papers, NLI) is unlocated; very short.
  • no. 402 Conde de Azevedo e Silva, Brussels → Ministry of Foreign Affairs, two telegrams in cipher 1904 — DigitArq: telegrams in cipher; no decipherment noted. Not digitised; not on DECODE.
  • no. 403 Telegram in cipher from St Petersburg to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lisbon 25 Oct 1904 — DigitArq: telegram in cipher; no decipherment noted. Not digitised; not on DECODE.

Register numbers place 4435 early (WWI era) and 23080/23197 later (1920s-30s). Whether the messages were read is not stated. Not digitised.
  • no. 683 The "Gulick message" signed "Honytre", still unsolved at Riverbank in Oct 1917, and the cipher letter found on Thomas Gulick Sept-Oct 1917 — Name-index cards: Riverbank (Fabyan) reports the 'Gulick message' signed Honytre still unsolved (10020-69, 2 Oct 1917). The same Riverbank card run lists monthly reports of 'undeciphered messages' (10020-64). Gulick held a suspicious cipher letter (9140-1369). Not the Tampico message (entry 674, 10020-60). The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.
  • no. 686 Document dug up near a post, believed to locate the James brothers' loot and signed 'Frank James': War Department cryptographers found no solution dug up 1931; MID correspondence 3 Sept-7 Dec 1931 — Cards (1931): photographs of the document went to MID. The Chief Signal Officer gave an 'interpretation', then the cryptographers were 'unable to arrive at any solution of the code'. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.
  • no. 688 Letter and map from 'Agent Pfeiffer' in signs taken for Slavic or Hungarian shorthand; MI-8 could not read them 21 Feb 1918 — Card: MI-8 was 'unable after exam' to add anything. The signs were thought to be shorthand. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.
  • no. 689 Intercepted letters in code from the Panama Canal Zone, including one to D. V. Kracker, Bogotá, that MI-8 could not decipher Feb 1918 — Card: the Intelligence Officer, Panama CZ, sent the letters; the Branch had 'not been able to decipher' them. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.
  • no. 697 German agent messages: two deciphered and the 'Tismera' message being worked through an old German shorthand system 9 Nov 1917 — Card: two messages deciphered; the 'Tismera' message was being deciphered by an old German shorthand system, 'very slow'. No later result on the card. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.

Kovacs, Valparaíso, to Buenos Aires: code messages (and Nunezant -> Morluk, Iquique), translation requested 23 Oct-21 Nov 1917 — Cards: translation of the messages requested; no result recorded. No solution recorded. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.
  • no. 702 Letter in cipher addressed to Cornelius K. Bettman, Barcelona, with a map thought to be of Havana harbour 1 Apr 1918 — Cards: the military attaché at Havana sent a photo copy of the cipher letter with the map. No solution recorded.   • no. 703 Code message to the Swiss consul at San Francisco; Weiskopf: 'almost impossible to decode a single message' 24 Mar 1917 — Case-file letter (OG 3337, 24 Mar 1917, Bureau to H. B. Hook, Nogales, Arizona): Victor Weiskopf, the Bureau's code expert, said one message could hardly be deciphered (it might be German, French or English) and asked for others in the same code. The message text was not found in the OCR of this roll; the Nogales report should carry the copy.
  • no. 710 Chicherin → Sukhanov (Vladivostok Soviet): telegram on routing Allied consular telegrams via Moscow, with code passages unread by AEF Siberia 4 May 1918 — AEF Siberia memorandum: 'The code and cipher section inform that they are not in position to solve by inspection the short passages of code contained in the message'; the key was presumed destroyed with Sukhanov's papers. The ciphertext itself is not on the reel; it may survive in the MID copy (RG 165) or the AEF intelligence files. The same memorandum describes 18 Allied telegrams (16 American, many 'wholly or partly in code') abstracted from the Vladivostok telegraph office; those are US/Allied traffic copies, not a separate candidate. Not in catalogue.json (known.py: no hits for Chicherin, Sukhanov).

Harper Papers) 1918-1920 — Finding aid: 'Memoranda on translations and code messages found with the Sisson documents (1918-1920)'. No cipher text or decipherment described. Not on DECODE; known.py finds the Sisson documents only as a cross-reference in an NARA triage row.

Partly in cipher, undeciphered). Not checked against the original or other editions; no DECODE check made (calendar entry, not a DECODE record).
  • no. 1004 Letter from Brussels with last paragraph in cipher, "undeciphered" (CSP Domestic Elizabeth 1595-97, p. 56) 12 Jun 1595 (Brussels) — Calendar says "the last paragraph in cipher, undeciphered". The Spanish/boors and Cardinal of Austria news fixes the date June 1595.
  • no. 1008 Sir Christopher Blunt's man to Sir Robert Cecil: merchandise allusions are a cipher, no key found Nov 1591 (day not given) — Calendar note only. The printed heading describes the sender rather than naming him.

The ciphertext itself is not identified in the calendar (probably SP 84 Germany or the Cypher Collections).

No decipherment noted. Not on DECODE; not in the repo (known.py, 28 Oct 2026).

  • no. 670 Intercepted Russian (Soviet) coded messages, 1931-1932 1931-1932 — SIS-era intercepts; Soviet systems of the period were mostly additive codes or one-time pads, so this may be out of hand-cipher scope. Not digitised.
  • no. 685 Nauen wireless code message that MI-8 judged 'not in any German code known to us' and indecipherable 13 May 1919 — Card: the Director of Naval Communications sent a Nauen code message to the Chief of Staff. Yardley's memo says it is 'not in any of Ger. codes known to us & is indecipherable'. Other Nauen intercepts of 1918 (10531-51, -103, -163; 4131-526, 25 messages) were deciphered. The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.

  • no. 706 French consular agent Las Palmas → Marine Casablanca, letter-cipher telegrams ('Nota num. 2-4') copied by an anonymous informant for the German naval attaché Madrid 22-28 Apr 1940 — Not on DECODE, not in the repo. No reading on file in the pages seen. The rest of the file (other intercepts, "unknown wireless signals" 1918) was not read through.

The MID correspondence file itself (RG 165, entry 65, MID 1917-41) is not digitised; only the index card (M1194/M912/M1474) is online.

Ridell, found in old papers July 1934 (Ask Adventure column, p. 124) — Unsolved per Schmeh (Cipherbrain 22 Apr 2018, revisiting a 2015 German post); analyses by Stefan Wagner and Norbert Biermann found nothing; a reader's 'Poe codebook' solution was built to fit and was rejected in the thread. About the catalogue

What is still in cipher in the digitised diplomatic volumes, and nobody has read. The first entries came from the French volumes on Gallica; the rest (51) from the DECODE database, every ciphertext record it marks non-decrypted or partly decrypted, grouped into letters and series and checked against this repository's own targets and Tomokiyo's list. A sweep of 22 Sept 2026 added candidates for new solves and outside reads: DECODE records never classified, letters Tomokiyo calls undeciphered while naming a key, Gallica notices and the printed calendars. On 14 Oct 2026 open items were pulled from Satoru’s Cryptoole index and checked against the repository. 1097 entries are counted targets, 14 are noted only. Class A means siblings with decipherment in the same volume, B a partial key or known family in print, C no key and no sibling. Entries read, partly read, resolved or found already in print are taken out of the catalogue and written up; those attempted here without a reading stay, tagged attempted, open. An entry a target folder is working on now is tagged in progress, read at each rebuild from the head of the folder’s NOTES.md, and its page links those notes.

Scores are judgements from catalogue descriptions and the literature, not from the leaves: 82 of 1111 entries have been viewed on the image, and each page carries the check that would confirm it is open. Data: catalogue.json · text: CATALOGUE.md · how to send a result: contribute.

How the scores were set

Importance asks what a full reading would add: 5 for a first-hand report of a major event by a principal witness (du Bellay in London 1529, Lanssac at the Polish election), 2 for routine business. Solvability asks whether the material online is enough: 5 when deciphered siblings of the same hand and year sit in the same volume, 1 for one short letter in an unknown language. Difficulty is the technical work at the keyboard: 1 for aligning a known sibling, 5 for a statistics-only attack on a large homophonic nomenclator. The default priority weights importance 0.4, solvability 0.35 and ease 0.25 (ease is 6 minus difficulty), rescaled to 0–10; change them under “More” above the table. Every score is a judgement made before viewing the leaf, so treat the order as a work plan, not a finding.

Checked: catalogue descriptions and item numbering; presence or absence of a decipherment item in each volume; shelfmarks from the IIIF manifests. For the DECODE entries: the record metadata and notes, key records from the same archive series, overlap with this repository's targets and with Tomokiyo's list. Entries tagged rule-scored were scored by a script from DECODE's metadata and not yet reviewed by hand. Verify each entry on the image and in the literature before attacking it.
